claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions in a copper matrix made by conventional powder metallurgy or infiltration.
Combining machine-learning optimization with transient liquid-phase sintering will precisely tune temperature ramp rate, dwell time, and applied pressure.
Machine-learning-guided transient liquid-phase sintering will produce uniform, void-free W–Cu interfaces.
Uniform, void-free W–Cu interfaces will improve thermal conductivity.
The proposed process will maintain mechanical durability under fusion-reactor service conditions.
The intervention optimizes interfacial reaction kinetics by systematically tuning sintering parameters.
Fusion-reactor components experience high heat or thermal flux and intense irradiation.
The process will enhance interfacial bonding and minimize defects between the tungsten and copper phases.
The machine-learning framework uses experimental and simulation data to predict favorable processing conditions.
The predicted conditions promote controlled formation of liquid copper and diffusion across preformed tungsten surfaces.
Controlled liquid-copper formation and interfacial diffusion reduce void formation and phase separation.
The proposed process will yield a more homogeneous and void-free microstructure than conventional spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, or direct infiltration.
The proposed material will have better thermal transport and irradiation-resistant mechanical durability than materials made by the named conventional methods.
Conventional spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying currently leave residual voids and phase separation in W–Cu composites.
The intervention will succeed only when the temperature remains below copper's boiling point while allowing sufficient interfacial diffusion.
The intervention is not expected to succeed if service conditions exceed thermal and irradiation fluxes typical of fusion reactors.
The exact processing window, scalability, and production-scale reproducibility are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The mechanism requires controlled Cu liquid-phase formation and a dwell near copper's melting region, but the conditions prescribe temperatures near yet below approximately 1085 °C while incorrectly identifying that value as copper's boiling point. Taken literally, remaining below approximately 1085 °C would not establish the stated molten-Cu phase.
